subject: Polity
topic: Directive Principles of State Policy — classification, enforceability, landmark amendments
description: DPSP (Arts 36-51): socialist, Gandhian, liberal directives — classification, non-justiciability vs fundamental rights, 42nd Amendment, Kesavananda Bharati, Minerva Mills cases.

questions.stem: Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are contained in which Part of the Indian Constitution?

options.option_text: Part IV (Articles 36-51) — DPSPs are in Part IV; Fundamental Rights are in Part III
Part III — Part III contains Fundamental Rights (Articles 12-35), not the DPSPs
Part V — Part V deals with the Union Executive (President, PM, Council of Ministers)
Part VI — Part VI deals with the State governments (Governor, CM, State Legislature)

questions.explanation: CONSTITUTION STRUCTURE: Part I: Union and Territory. Part II: Citizenship. Part III: FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS (Arts 12-35). Part IV: DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES (Arts 36-51). Part IVA: Fundamental Duties (Art 51A — added by 42nd Amendment 1976). Part V: Union Executive. DPSP CHARACTERISTICS: (1) Non-justiciable — cannot be enforced by courts. (2) Positive obligations on the State. (3) Borrowed from Irish Constitution. (4) Welfare state framework. PURPOSE: even though unenforceable, they guide legislation and governance; courts consider them in interpreting Fundamental Rights. PYQ: DPSPs are in Part IV in IBPS PO, SSC polity — standard 1-marker.

questions.stem: Article 40 of the Indian Constitution directs the State to organise village panchayats. This DPSP is classified under which category?

options.option_text: Gandhian directive — Art 40 reflects Gandhi's vision of village self-governance (gram swaraj)
Socialist directive — socialist DPSPs relate to economic equality, minimum wages, right to work
Liberal-intellectual directive — liberal directives relate to education, environment, international peace
Fundamental duty — fundamental duties are in Part IVA (Art 51A), not Part IV DPSPs

questions.explanation: THREE CATEGORIES OF DPSPs: SOCIALIST (economic/social justice): Arts 38, 39, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47. Examples: equal pay, right to work, living wages, maternity relief. GANDHIAN (based on Gandhi's ideas): Arts 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48. Examples: village panchayats, cottage industries, welfare of SCs/STs, prohibition, cow protection. LIBERAL-INTELLECTUAL (international relations, education): Arts 44, 45, 48A, 49, 50, 51. Examples: UCC (Art 44), free education (Art 45, before Art 21A), environment protection (Art 48A), separation of judiciary (Art 50), international peace (Art 51). ART 40 = village panchayats = Gandhian. Implemented by 73rd Amendment (1992) — Panchayati Raj. PYQ: Art 40 + Gandhian category in UPSC, IBPS PO polity.

questions.stem: In the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court held that the relationship between DPSPs and Fundamental Rights is:

options.option_text: Complementary — DPSPs and Fundamental Rights should be harmoniously construed; neither is absolutely superior
DPSPs are supreme over Fundamental Rights and can override them entirely (not this) instead
Fundamental Rights are always superior and DPSPs are merely political promises with no legal weight
They are completely separate and courts must never consider DPSPs when adjudicating Fundamental Rights

questions.explanation: HISTORICAL EVOLUTION: EARLY VIEW (State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan, 1951): Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSPs. 42nd AMENDMENT (1976): gave DPSPs primacy over Arts 14, 19 — Indira Gandhi tried to make DPSPs override Fundamental Rights. MINERVA MILLS CASE (1980): SC struck down the 42nd Amendment provision giving DPSPs primacy over FRs — ruled that perfect harmony between FRs and DPSPs is part of the basic structure; neither can be sacrificed for the other. KESAVANANDA BHARATI (1973): established basic structure doctrine — FRs and DPSPs are like two wheels of the chariot of Indian democracy. CURRENT POSITION: they must be harmoniously construed; laws implementing DPSPs can restrict FRs if they don't violate basic structure. PYQ: DPSP vs Fundamental Rights relationship in UPSC Prelims.

questions.stem: Article 44 of the Indian Constitution directs the State to secure for citizens a Uniform Civil Code (UCC). This Article is significant because:

options.option_text: It aims for a single set of civil laws (marriage, divorce, inheritance) applicable to all citizens regardless of religion
It immediately makes all personal laws unconstitutional and replaces them with a single statute
It only applies to Hindu citizens; Muslim, Christian, and Parsi personal laws are outside its scope
It has already been implemented across India following the 44th Constitutional Amendment (not this)

questions.explanation: ART 44 (UCC): The State shall endeavour to secure for citizens a UNIFORM CIVIL CODE throughout India. CIVIL CODE covers: marriage, divorce, adoption, inheritance, succession, maintenance. CURRENT SITUATION: India has different personal laws for different religions (Hindu Personal Law, Muslim Personal Law, Christian Personal Law, Parsi Personal Law). UCC = replace all with ONE secular code. STATUS: NOT YET IMPLEMENTED at national level (as of early 2026). EXCEPTION: Goa has a common civil code (inherited from Portuguese rule). DEBATES: Muslim community resistance (religious freedom); supporters argue UCC necessary for gender equality and national integration. SHAH BANO CASE (1985): triggered the UCC debate — SC awarded maintenance to a Muslim divorced woman under CrPC; Parliament reversed via Muslim Women Act 1986. PYQ: Art 44 + UCC significance in UPSC, IBPS PO.

questions.stem: Article 48A of the Constitution (added by 42nd Amendment 1976) directs the State to protect and improve the environment. This is classified under which DPSP category?

options.option_text: Liberal-intellectual directive — environmental protection alongside international peace, education, culture
Gandhian directive — Gandhian directives focus on rural India and cottage industries, not the environment
Socialist directive — socialist directives deal with economic equality, not ecological protection
Emergency directive — there is no separate 'emergency directive' category within the DPSPs

questions.explanation: ART 48A: State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife. CLASSIFICATION: LIBERAL-INTELLECTUAL directive. 42ND AMENDMENT (1976): added Art 48A (environment) and Art 51A(g) (citizen's fundamental duty to protect environment). COMPLEMENTARY PROVISION: Art 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty): it shall be the duty of every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife. JUDICIAL EXPANSION: Art 21 (right to life) interpreted to include right to a clean environment (Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar, 1991). ENVIRONMENT PROTECTION ACT 1986: enacted partly fulfilling Art 48A. PYQ: Art 48A + 42nd Amendment + environment in UPSC, IBPS PO polity.

questions.stem: Article 39(b) and 39(c) of the Constitution direct the State to ensure equitable distribution of material resources and prevent concentration of wealth. These are implemented through which mechanism?

options.option_text: Laws on land reform, nationalisation, and progressive taxation — Parliament has used Art 39(b)/(c) to justify these
Direct cash transfers to citizens by the Union Government using constitutional authority under Art 39
Court-mandated redistribution of private property by judicial order under Art 39 (not this)
Art 39 is unimplemented; it has no corresponding legislation since DPSPs are non-justiciable

questions.explanation: ART 39(B): material resources of the community should be so distributed as best to subserve the common good. ART 39(C): economic system should not result in concentration of wealth and means of production to common detriment. IMPLEMENTATION: (1) ZAMINDARI ABOLITION ACTS (1950s) — broke up large landholdings. (2) BANK NATIONALISATION (1969) — 14 major banks nationalised; justified under Art 39. (3) PRIVY PURSE ABOLITION (1971). (4) URBAN LAND CEILING ACTS. PROPERTY BANK CASE (2024): 9-judge bench revisited whether private property is 'material resources of community' under Art 39(b). CONSTITUTION PROTECTION: Ninth Schedule protects certain laws from judicial review (Art 31B). PYQ: Art 39(b)/(c) + implementation in UPSC GS-2, IBPS PO polity.

questions.stem: The 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) converted which DPSP into a Fundamental Right?

options.option_text: Free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 — Art 45 DPSP converted to Art 21A Fundamental Right
Uniform Civil Code — Art 44 remains a DPSP; it has not been converted into a Fundamental Right
Equal pay for equal work — Art 39(d) remains a DPSP and has not been elevated to a Fundamental Right
Village panchayats — Art 40 remains a DPSP; panchayats are in Part IX (73rd Amendment)

questions.explanation: 86TH AMENDMENT (2002): most significant recent Fundamental Right addition. CREATED: Art 21A — right of children aged 6-14 to free and compulsory education (Fundamental Right). CONVERTED: the old Art 45 DPSP (free education up to 14) was REPLACED with a narrower DPSP (early childhood care for children below 6). Also added Fundamental Duty: Art 51A(k) — parent/guardian's duty to provide education to child. ENABLING LEGISLATION: Right to Education Act (RTE Act) 2009 — operationalised Art 21A. RTE PROVISIONS: no capitation fee, no screening of child/parent for admission, 25% seats reserved for economically weaker sections in private schools, no detention till Class 8. PYQ: 86th Amendment + Art 21A in UPSC Prelims, IBPS PO polity — 1x per year.
